title: Pavement spreads unabated across Chesapeake Bay watershed, threatening streams
summary: The Chesapeake Bay watershed is adding enough runoff-inducing pavement and buildings every year to completely cover an area the size of Staunton, Virginia, new data shows.
content:
By Timothy B. Wheeler

The Chesapeake Bay Journal

The Chesapeake Bay watershed is adding enough runoff-inducing pavement and buildings every year to completely cover an area the size of Staunton, Virginia, new data shows.

A recently completed analysis of high-resolution aerial surveys of the six-state watershed finds that the amount of land covered by roads, rooftops, parking lots and other impervious surfaces expanded annually by 13,226 acres, or more than 20 square miles, from 2013 through 2021.

The rate of increase grew slightly over that eight-year period, the analysis shows. The end result: More than 100,000 acres, or about 160 square miles of pavement and hard structures added to the landscape — almost enough to cover Richmond, Norfolk and Hampton, Virginia, combined.

The data comes from a federally funded effort to map and track changes in land use and land cover across the Bay watershed every four years. Collaborators on the project include the nonprofit Chesapeake Conservancy, the U.S. Geological Survey, the University of Vermont and the federal-state Chesapeake Bay Program.

The surveys, which capture aerial imagery of the landscape at a 1-meter resolution, help analysts monitor the conversion of forest and farmland to development. With the help of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, the collaborators also have compiled “hyper-resolution” maps of rivers, streams and wetlands in unprecedented detail.

The finding that impervious surfaces have continued to spread unabated, though, suggests that state and local governments have yet to halt, much less reverse, the harm to the Bay and its tributaries done by development’s hardened footprint.

Impervious surfaces are widely recognized as killers of water quality and aquatic life. When rain falls on roads, rooftops and sidewalks, rather than soaking into the ground, it runs off and carries pollutants like excess fertilizer, pet waste, toxic chemicals and litter to the nearest waterway. Those hard surfaces also absorb the sun’s radiation, heating the stormwater runoff and raising stream temperatures — often to a degree that many fish, amphibians and aquatic insects can no longer live there.

According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the streets, rooftops and other impervious surfaces in a typical city block generate more than five times as much runoff as a similar sized patch of forest.

But urban waterways aren’t the only ones harmed by impervious surfaces. Stream health begins to decline when pavement and buildings cover as little as 5-10% of a watershed, research has shown. Banks start to erode, and brook trout, which are highly sensitive to disturbance, vanish. Salamanders and mussels dwindle.

When development spreads hardened surfaces over more than 20% of a watershed, streams lose all but the most pollution-tolerant fish and aquatic creatures.

Pavement and buildings have been covering the Bay watershed faster than its population has been growing for decades. From 1990 to 2007, according to the Bay Program, impervious surfaces associated with development of single-family homes increased by about 34%, while the population increased by 18%.

The aerial surveys conducted in 2017-18 spotted 3,000 square miles of impervious cover. That’s just 4.75% of the Bay watershed’s land area, seemingly below that 5% threshold for impacting water quality. But pavement and buildings aren’t evenly distributed. They are rampant in densely developed cities, but there are also many streams and portions of streams in the spreading suburbs of Maryland and Virginia where more than 20% of their watersheds are covered with pavement and buildings.

Peter Claggett, a research geographer with the U.S. Geological Survey who’s helped analyze the data garnered from the high-resolution aerial surveys, said he was surprised by the pace at which impervious cover continued to expand. He said he expected slower growth, especially in the first four-year period between surveys, because housing development was still relatively slow in the wake of the 2007-2008 recession.

But Claggett said he noticed a change in the type of development that puts the biggest impervious footprint on the landscape.

“It’s warehouses, data centers, chicken houses,” he said. “Those are the kind of buildings we’ve seen that are new. And you also have the solar panel arrays.”

Though some have suggested solar development could cover hundreds of thousands of acres, the 2021-22 surveys spotted only about 4,400 acres of arrays across the six-state watershed, nearly two-thirds of that in Virginia.

But with legislation in Virginia and Maryland encouraging solar development, a number of large projects have been built since then, and hundreds more are on the drawing table — though many may not proceed for a variety of reasons.

Though they are not as solidly impervious as pavement or buildings, ground-mounted solar installations can still increase stormwater runoff and soil erosion. In June, Virginia imposed new regulations that require some large utility-scale solar projects to reduce or mitigate their impacts.

“We’re going to be tracking solar for the foreseeable future,” Claggett said.

States and local governments have attempted to minimize the damage to some streams from impervious surfaces. They have adopted stormwater management requirements and development standards aimed at reducing runoff and filtering out pollutants.

“If you know where your most sensitive watersheds are, you can focus more on land conservation activities, stream buffers [and the like],” said David Wood, executive director of the Timonium-based nonprofit Chesapeake Stormwater Network. For the last 15 years, Maryland regulators have advocated “environmental site design” in planning development, which calls for corralling rainfall and getting it to soak into the soil rather than run off into the nearest stream.

“What we’re seeing is [that it] it helps,” Wood said. “It makes a difference, but it doesn’t offset the growth entirely.”

While the harmful effects of impervious surfaces are widely recognized, the Chesapeake Bay Program has never formally set a goal of reducing it or limiting its spread. The 2014 Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement, signed by all six Bay watershed states and the District of Columbia, pledged only to “evaluate policy options, incentives and planning tools” that local officials might use to curb forest loss and reduce the spread of impervious surfaces.

The draft revision of that agreement now being considered strikes much the same note, pledging “land use decision support” in the form of “relevant and actionable land use information” be made available to organizations and communities involved in planning future growth and development.
